parties:
State ------ Appellant
vs.
Ershad Ali Sikder and others ------ Condemned Prisoners
full_judgment:
23. Central evidence against condemned prisoners, appellants and other accused persons consisted of evidence of approver PW 1 Noor Alam. Eye-witnesses PWs 1, 3, 4, 5, 7, 9, 10 and 14 claimed to have witnessed the incident. PWs 21, 22, 31 and 33 have been examined to corroborate ocular evidences of above stated eye-witnesses. 

 24. Besides ocular evidence, prosecution in proof of its case, put on record Judicial Confessional Statement recorded under section 164 of The Code (Exhibit 3), Post Mortem Report (Exhibit 9), Injury Certificate (Exhibit 10), Seizure list evidencing seizure of Material Exhibits, Suzuki Motor Cycle Yamaha and parts of Car and other incriminating articles. 

 25. On conclusion of evidence condemned prisoners, appellants and accused persons were examined under section 342 of The Code. 

 26. Learned trial Judge on discussion and consideration of evidences and materials on record found that in furtherance of common intention to kill Khaled accused Ershad Ali Sikder, Faruque alias Jamai Faruque, LM  Liaquat Ali Lashkar, Idris Jamai and Nasir Khan with Crowbar (শাবাল), Iron Rod etc. caused the death of Khaled and prosecution successfully proved charge of sections 302/34 of Penal Code. Learned trial Judge again held that Ershad Ali Sikder, Faruque alias Jamai Faruque, LM Liaquat Ali Lashkar, Nasir Khan, Idris Jamai, Sentu alias Hindu Sheikh, Yousuf Ali alias. Yousuf, Younus, Ashraf Boro Miah, Md Mannan alias Mona, Ayub Ali Munshi, Kuju Altaf caused injury of grievous nature upon Monir (PW 3) and they committed offence of sections 325/34 of Penal Code and prosecution successfully proved charge against them. Learned trial Judge in view of imposition of sentence of offence of sections 302/34 of Penal Code upon Ershad Ali Sikder, LM Liaquat Ali Lashkar, Faruque alias Jamai Faruque, Idris Jamai and Nasir Khan did not award any separate sentence for offence of sections 325/34 of Penal Code. Learned trial Judge in rendering decision took into account laws embodied in sections 133 and 114(b) of The Evidence Act and, also, a decision in Atar Ali vs State, 44 DLR 478. 

 First Information Report is the earliest account of the case and it may not be last word of a case but it is the foundation of a case. From evidence of Sub-Inspector of Police (PW 33) it came out that GD No. 1353. dated 16-5-93 was registered and Babul made GD -that GD was required to be treated as First Information Report. Prosecution case commenced on the strength of First Information Report lodged by Informant PW 2 got no leg to stand and whole prosecution case fell to ground. Nurjahan Begum vs State, 1988 BLD 389 and Muslimuddin and others vs State, 38 DLR (AD) 311 have been referred to in support of the contention advanced. 

 It is true that PW 33 in his evidence stated that one GD had been registered and Professor Babul (PW 13) was the author of that GD Entry. No investigation commenced on the basis of that GD Entry as came out from the mouth of PW 33. GD Entry did not come to the court. No attempt had been made even by the accused persons to call for GD Entry at least to know the contents and quality of that GD Entry. Even the alleged authority of GD Entry Babul (PW 13) was not at all confronted with the alleged GD Entry allegedly registered by him with Police Station. Investigation of the case started on the basis of First Information Report laid by Informant PW 2 who is no other than full sister or injured witness PW 3.  First Information Report lodged by Informant PW 2, though, allegedly appeared to have been latter in point of time, is not to be flung to the wind in view of laying of an alleged GD Entry and First Information Report laid by Informant PW 2 is not at all liable to be excluded as being hit by section 162 of The Code. 

 39. Repelling the said contention it has been contended from side of State that PW 1 had chosen to be approver and accordingly he presented a petition through Superintendent of Jail and the said petition was forwarded to Public Prosecutor. Assistant Public Prosecutor conducting case filed the said petition before learned trial Judge for according Noor Alam permission to give testimony as approver and Noor Alam as approver PW 1 gave evidence making disclosure of acts of accused persons. 

 42. A reading of section 337 of The Code demonstrates that the dominant object of the section is that offender of heinous and grave offence does not go unpunished and scoot free. To put it differently, the object of the section is to allow pardon to be tendered in cases where grave offence is committed by several persons and with the aid of evidence of a person pardoned the offence is brought home to rest. The purpose of the section is to obtain evidence of a person supposed to have been directly or indirectly concerned in a privy to an offence during investigation, inquiry or trial. The condition for tender of such person is that the person is to make a full and true disclosure of whole circumstances within his knowledge relating to offence. 

 44. PW 1 Noor Alam was pardoned with condition of making a full and true disclosure of whole incident and PW 1 as witness made disclosure of offence committed by accused persons. In trial PW 1 was discharged. No illegality and legal infirmity are manifested in giving testimony on administration of oath by approver PW 1 Noor Alam and evidence of approver PW 1 Noor Alam is admissible. 

 45. Section 339 of The Code enjoins that a certificate from Public Prosecutor. PW 1 Noor Alam, presented a petition through Superintendent of Jail to be an approver and said application had been forwarded to Public Prosecutor and Assistant Public Prosecutor filed the said petition before learned Judge to accord Noor Alam permission to give evidence in court. The petition presented by learned Assistant Public Prosecutor before Judge can be very much characterised as a certificate issued by Public Prosecutor. It, thus cannot be suggested that provision contained in section 339(1) of The Code had not been complied with. It is observed here that acceptance of this objection raised from side of condemned prisoners and appellants would simply promote technical plea which would adversely affect dispensation of justice. In Angur vs State, 41 DLR 66 is quite distinguishable in the fact and circumstances of the case and, as such, got no manner of application. 

 46. It is emphatically indicated here that even if the evidence of approver PW 1 Noor Alam is excluded, there are other evidences coming from mouth of eye witnesses to occurrence connecting perpetrators of crime in causing death to Khaled and injuries of grievous nature to Monir (PW 3). Contention No.2 having been devoid of any substance stands ruled out. 

 Contention highlighted is that confession of PW 1 Noor Alam was not made in accordance with sections 164 and 364 of The Code and certificate and memorandum were not given in the hand of learned Magistrate. In his evidence PW 1 Noor Alain did not state that he could identify accused persons by electric bulb which he did not state in his confessional statement recorded under section 164 of The Code and recognition of the accused persons through electric bulb is to be left out of consideration, it is further submitted. This contention does not hold water and stands rejected outright. 

 48. Examination of the confessional statement does not at all indicate that requirements of law embodied in section 164 read with section 364 of The Code had not been at all complied with and there had been any breach thereof. Confessing accused Noor Alam stood on witness box as PW 1 and made true disclosure of the incident. Learned Magistrate, First Class, who recorded Confessional statement, was examined as PW 6 and he stated in his evidence that requirements of law had been complied with. True it is that in confessional statement he did not mention of any electric bulb but he mentioned of Mercury light in front of Ice Factory of condemned prisoner Ershad Ali Sikder with which bank of the river was quite visible. In his evidence before Court as PW 1 Noor Alam stated that there had been lights of 100 power bulb in 2/3 shops. It well nigh to remember that evidence on witness box is the legal evidence and confessional statement is not a legal evidence. Sections 8 and 9 of The Evidence Act can conveniently be pressed in aid in this context. Moreover, the accused persons were well known to PW 1 Noor Alam and there was no difficulty on his part to recognise and identify accused persons who committed the offence. 

 Out of fifty-six (56) charge-sheet witnesses only thirty-four (34) witnesses had been examined and neighboring people, shop keepers were not examined and prosecution withheld important witnesses and had important and, independent witnesses would have been examined, they would not have supported prosecution case. Section 114(g) of The Evidence Act has been pressed into service in support of contention raised. 

 50. It is no doubt true that prosecution is to produce witnesses who are essential to unfolding of narrative on which prosecution case is based but it cannot be laid down as a Rule that if there are large number of witnesses noted in charge-sheet the prosecution is bound to call and examine each and every one of those witnesses. Material witnesses considered necessary by the prosecution for divulging prosecution story alone need be produced without unnecessary and redundant multiplication of witnesses. In this case enough number of witnesses, thirty-four (34) in number, had been examined in proof of prosecution case. Prosecution produced eye-witnesses including injured witness Monir (PW 3) on witness box and these witnesses are quite natural and competent. Occurrence took place at about 9-00 to 9-30 AM and it could not be expected that good number of other independent witnesses would be present on the scene of occurrence only to witness the occurrence. Mere fact that prosecution failed to examine other witnesses cannot be a manifestation that such witnesses were unwilling to support prosecution case. Non production of such witnesses at the trial did not at all destroy evidences produced and adduced by other witnesses. Learned Counsels could not show how the prosecution story was rendered less trustworthy as a result of non-production of other witnesses noted in charge sheet. Moreover, nowadays citizens of the land who are cited witness do not dare to stand on witness box to give testimony against the offenders and do not want to invite enmity for fear of their lives and they, also, incur apprehension that they might even be snubbed out of the world. There is general apathy of public not to involve themselves and remain aloof from offenders and courts. One cannot ignore the hardship with which Investigating Agencies have to discharge their duties in collecting evidences to unveil truth. This ground reality must not be overlooked. Condemned prisoners and appellants cannot get any benefit of section 114(g) of The Evidence Act. The contention carries no merit and the same stands rejected. 

 Discrepancies, material contradictions and omissions occurring in testimonies of prosecution witnesses made prosecution case doubtful and out of court and a verdict of acquittal was required to have been passed upon condemned prisoners and appellants. Discrepancies, contradictions and omissions which occurred in the testimonies of PWs 3, 4, 5, 7, 10 and 14 had been pointed out and brought to our notice. It is true that discrepancies, contradictions and omissions occurred in testimonies of some of the eye-witnesses and some accused persons can be benefited by discrepancies, contradictions and omissions and this will be dealt with later on at the time of scanning evidences of prosecution witnesses and extracting grain from chaff and benefit shall be given to accused persons who can derive benefit. 

 Much stress has been laid in bringing home contention that the case is of no evidence and prosecution case rested on testimony of PW 1 Noor Alam only. This contention can be brushed aside without much difficulty. PW 1 Noor Alam as approver made a disclosure of picture and circumstances leading to death of Khaled and causing injuries of grievous nature to Monir (PW 3). PW 1 stated the names of authors of offence. Testimony of PW 1 Noor Alam could not be even discredited by gruelling cross-examination from side of accused persons. Besides the evidence of PW 1 Noor Alam, prosecution case stood proved by direct ocular evidence of a good number of eye-witnesses who witnessed the incident. Ocular evidence of eye-witnesses had been corroborated by medical evidence and other legal evidences. We are not at all impressed by contention so raised. 

 (i). whether awarding of conviction and consequently sentence upon the condemned prisoners, appellants and other accused persons are well founded on law, evidences and materials on record and in safe dispensation of Criminal Justice. 

 "A "reasonable doubt" is such a doubt as would cause a reasonable and prudent man in the graver and more important affairs of life to pause and hesitate to act upon the truth of the matter charged. But a reasonable doubt is not a mere possibility of innocence, nor a caprice, shadow, or speculation as to innocence not arising out of the evidence or the want of it." 

 "It is not mere possible doubt, because everything relating to human affairs and depending upon moral evidence is open to some possible or imaginary doubt. It is that state of the case which, after the entire comparison and consideration of all the evidence, leaves the minds of the jurors in that consideration that they cannot say they feel an abiding conviction to a moral certainty of the truth of the charge." 

 56. In common parlance Benefit of doubt means an advantage or behoove of doubt. Reasonable doubt must be a doubt, arising from the evidences or from the want of evidences and cannot be an imaginary doubt or conjectures unrelated to evidence. Doubts which are real, genuine, well founded, which a normal man with normal intelligence in a given circumstances would normally harbor are doubts that come within the fold of Reasonable doubt entitling one to benefit of doubt. It is, also, to be remembered that the dangers of exaggerated devotion to Rule of Benefit of Doubt at the expense of social defence and to soothing sentiment that all acquittals are good regardless of the justice to victim and society, demand special emphasis in contemporary context of escalating crime. The golden thread of proof beyond Reasonable doubt should not be morbidly stretched to embrace any degree of doubt. If guilty person goes scot free and stands acquitted on the concept of Benefit of Reasonable doubt Justice System shall break down and citizens of the land shall lose confidence in Judicial System. 

 58. The fate of conviction and consequential sentence is inevitably founded upon our assessment of facts and intensive appraisal of our legal survey of evidence and materials on record which are as hereunder: 

 (i). Evidence of approver PW 1 Noor Alarm 

 (ii). Ocular evidence of eye-witnesses furnished by PWs 3, 4, 5, 7, 9, 10 and 14. 

 (iii). Evidence of PW 21, PW 22 and Medical Evidence that is Post Mortem Report of deceased Khaled (Exhibit 9) and Injury Certificate of injured witness PW 3 Monir (Exhibit 10) 

 (iv). Confessional Statement of approver PW 1 Noor Alam (Exhibit 3) and evidence of PW 6 who recorded Confessional Statement under section 164 of The Code. 

 59. It is pointed here that while appreciating evidence of a witness, approach must be whether evidence of the witness read as a whole appeared to have a ring of truth. It is undoubtedly necessary for the court to scrutinise the evidence, more particularly keeping in view the deficiencies, drawback and infirmities pointed out in evidence as whole and to evaluate them to find out whether it is against the general tenor of evidence. Court has to judge the evidence by yardstick of probabilities, its intrinsic worth and animus of witness. It is Court's duty to shift evidence separating truth from falsehood, grain from the chaff and come to its own conclusion about the guilt or innocence of the person accused of an offence. 

 60. Evidence of accomplice PW 1 Noor Alam 

 The word "accomplice" has not been defined in the Evidence Act. It is generally understood that an accomplice means a guilty associate or partner in crime. An accomplice by becoming an approver becomes a prosecution witness. Section 133 and illustration (b) to section 114 of The Evidence Act deal with the law relating to an accomplice evidence. An accomplice namely, a guilty associate in crime, is a competent witness. Section 133 lays down that the conviction based upon uncorroborated testimony of an accomplice is not illegal but Rule of guidance and Rule of prudence indicated in illustration (b) to section 114 of The Evidence Act has resulted in the settled practice to require corroboration of an evidence of an accomplice which is now virtually assumed force of Rule of law. In interpretation of section 133 and illustration (b) to section 114 of The Evidence Act courts have laid down that an approver's evidence has to satisfy a double test. 

 (i). His evidence must be reliable 

 (ii). His evidence should be corroborated by other evidences. 

 61. In respect of the evidence of an approver the law as stated in King vs Baskerville, (1916) 2KB 658 is, that where on the trial of an accused, evidences given against him by accomplice, the corroboration which the common law requires, is corroboration in some material particulars tending to show that the accused committed the crime charged. It is not enough that corroboration shows the witness to have, told the truth in matters not connected with the guilt of the accused. In Davies vs Director of Public Prosecutions, (1954) 1 All ER 507 it was observed that in a criminal trial where a person who was an accomplice gave evidence on behalf of the prosecution, although the jury might convict him on his evidence, it was, dangerous to do so unless his evidence is corroborated; this rule although a rule of practice now had the force of a rule of law. In Srinivas Mall vs Emperor, AIR 1947 PC 135 the Pivy Council held that no doubt the evidence of accomplices ought as a rule to be regarded with suspicion. The degree of suspicion which will attach to it, must however, vary according to the extent .and nature of the complicity; sometimes the accomplice is not a. willing participant in the offence but a victim of it. When, the accomplices act under a form of pressure which it would' require some firmness to resist, reliance can be placed on their uncorroborated evidence. In Bhuboni Sahu vs King, (AIR 1949 PC 257 = 50 CriLJ 8715=2 DLR (PC) 39 Privy Council observed: 

 "The courts should be slow to depart from the rule of prudence, based on long experience, which requires some independent evidence implicating the particular accused. The danger of acting upon accomplice evidence is not merely that the accomplice is on his own admission a man of bad character who took part in the offence and afterwards to save himself betrayed his former associates and who has placed himself in a position in which he can hardly fail to have a strong bias in favour of the prosecution; the real danger is that he is telling a story which in its general outline is true; and it is easy for him to work into the story matter which is untrue." 

 Law, thus, mandates that the evidence of an accomplice does not demand outright rejection if there is no corroboration but, though, there is no legal necessity to seek corroboration of an accomplice evidence it is desirable that the court seeks reassuring circumstances to satisfy Judicial conscience that evidence is true. 

 62. PW 1 Noor Alam in his evidence attributed the act of causing injuries of grievous nature on PW 3 Munir to Ershad Ali Sikder. PW 1 assigned act of causing injuries of grievous nature causing death to Khaled to Ershad Ali Sikder, Faruque alias Jamai Faruque, LM Liaquat Ali Lashkar, Idris Jamai and Nasir Khan. PW 1's evidence attributing authorship to Ershad Ali Sikder in causing death to Khaled stood corroborated by evidence of PWs 3, 4, 7, 9, 10 and 14 and; also, the evidence of PW 21. PW l's evidence connecting Ershad Ali Sikder, Faruque alias Jamai Faruque, LM Liaquat Ali Lashker and Nasir Khan in causing injuries to PW 3 Munir, also, stood corroborated by evidences of PWs 3, 4, 5, 7, 9, 10 and 14 and, also, evidence of PW 22, Evidence of PW 1 Noor Alam satisfied the test of reliability. 

 63. II. Ocular evidence of eye-witnesses: 

 (a) PW 3 Munir who is injured witness in his evidence fixed Ershad Ali Sikder as the culprit who caused injury on his head by rifle. He, also, implicated Jamai Faruque, LM Liaquat Ali Lashkar, Amir Khan, Kasai Ayub Munshi and Sentu alias Hindu Sheikh in mounting assault upon his person. PW 3 Munir raised his finger at Ershad Ali Sikder, Faruque alias Jamai Faruque, Liaquat Ali Loshkor, Nasir Khan, Kasai Ayub Munshi, Mona, Sentu alias Hindu Sheikh, Babul and Latif as authors of causing death of Khaled. PW 3 Munir did not state of any assault upon PW 4 Syed Chainul Islam Chayan. 

 (b) PW 4 Syed Chainul Islam Chayan in his evidence stated that Ershad Ali Sikder with rifle laid strike on head of his brother Munir (PW 3). Further testimony is that LM Liaquat Ali Lashkar, Faruque alias Jamai Faruque, Idris Jamai, Joynal, Latif, Ashraf Baro Mia, Babu, Babul, Younus, Yousuf, Nasir Khan, Sentu alias Hindu Sheikh and Ripon laid attack upon him and other persons. Assault with weapon upon Khaled and causing his death had been attributed only to Ershad Ali Sikder by this PW 3 Munir and not to anybody else. 

 (c) PW 5 Mohammad Ali in his testimony testified that Ershad Ali Sikder with rifle in his hand hit on head of Munir (PW 3) and Ershad Ali Sikder, LM Liaquat Ali Lashkar, Faruque alias Jamai Faruque, Nasir Khan, Idris Jamai, Ashraf Baro Miah, Ayub Ali Munshi, Motiur Rahman alias Moti, Md Mannan alias Mona, Babu, Babul, Sentu alias Hindu Sheikh, Altaf, Latif, Jafor Gazi, Younus, Yousuf and others encircled and assaulted Munir (PW 3) and broke his legs. It is his evidence that accused persons laid Khaled on the ground and smashed Khaled's hands and legs and Ershad Ali Sikder jumped/ danced on the chest of Khaled. PW 5 Mohammad Ali depicted only Ershad Ali Sikder as the perpetrator of crime. 

 (d) PW 7 Abul Hossain in his evidence stated that Ershad Ali Sikder with cut rifle in hand laid assault on the head of Munir (PW 3) and LM Liaquat Ali Lashkar, Faruque alias Jamai Faruque, Idris Jamai, Ashraf Baro Mia, Ayub Ali Munshi and Nasir Khan with Rod, Crowbar, Pairan, etc. bruised his two legs. PW 7 stated that Ershad Ali Sikder jumped/danced on chest of Khaled and started breaking his hand and feet with 20 KG weight Pairan PW 7, also, fixed only Ershad as the perpetrator of crime. 

 (e) PW 9 Ashit Barun Biswas in his evidence stated that Ershad Ali Sikder with Faruque alias Jamai Faruque, Ayub Ali Munshi, LM Liaquat Ali Lashkar, Nasir Khan, Idris Jamai, Ashraf Baro Mia came down and Ershad Ali Sikder with but of rifle hit on Munir (PW 3). PW 9 further stated Ershad Ali Sikder with Crowbar and other weapons assaulted Khaled and danced on chest of Khaled. PW 9 fixed only Ershad Ali Sikder as offender for causing death to Khaled. 

 (g) PW 14 Shaikh Parvez in his evidence stated that Ershad Ali Sikder with a rifle in his hand laid strike on the head of Munir (PW 3) and at the command of Ershad Ali Sikder accused persons laid Munir (PW 3) on ground and smashed his legs with Crowbar, Pairan etc. Further evidence is that the accused persons caught hold of Khaled and Ershad Ali Sikder ordered to eliminate Khaled. 

 64. Substratum of evidences of eye-witnesses PWs 1, 3, 4, 5, 7, 9, 10 and 14 demonstrates that all the eye-witnesses pointed their fingers. at Ershad Ali Sikder as the author of causing death of Khaled and testimonies of eye-witnesses in respect of Ershad Ali Sikder appeared to be consistent and do no appear to have suffered from discrepancies and infirmity but so far as condemned prisoners Faruque alias Jamai Faruque and LM Liakot Ali Lashkar and other appellants and accused persons are concerned testimonies appeared to have suffered from discrepancies, inconsistencies and infirmities. 

 66. Careful and meticulous examination of evidences of approver PW 1 Noor Alam, eye-witnesses, PWs 3, 4, 5, 7, 9, 10 and 14 indicates that evidences in connecting Ershad Ali Sikder, Faruque alias Jamai Faruque, LM Liaquat Ali Lashkar and Nasir Khan in causing injuries of grievous nature on Munir (PW 3) are consistent and their evidences in respect to appellants Idris Jamai, Yousuf, Abdul Latif, Matiur Rahman alias Moti, Sentu alias Hindu Sheikh and other convicts Md Mannan alias Mona, Ashraf Baro Miah, Ayub Ali Munshi and Kuju Altaf suffer from inconsistencies, discrepancies and infirmities. 

 67. III. Medical Evidence: 

 PW 21 Dr Golam Mortuza who performed autopsy on the body of Khaled found five (5) items of injuries on his body. PW 22 Dr Gazi Mizanur Rahman who examined injured witness PW 3 Munir found three (3) items of injuries on the person of Munir (PW 3) and issued certificate. The evidence of approver PW 1 Noor Alam and ocular evidence of eye-witnesses furnished by PWs 3, 4, 5, 7, 9,10 and 14 stand corroborated by evidence of PWs 21 and 22. Medical evidence, Post Mortem Examination Report (Exhibit 9) and Injury Certificate (Exhibit 10) lent support to evidences of eye-witnesses and evidence of PW 1 Noor Alam. 

 Confession is not statutorily defined either under The Code of Criminal Procedure nor The Evidence Act but the expression is well established. Confession is nothing but admission of guilt by the accused. Confessions are of two types. 

 69. Judicial Confession is made before a Magistrate and the same is recorded under section 164 read with section 364 of The Code and we are concerned with Judicial Confession only. Confession of a co-accused is not an evidence as defined in section 3 of The Evidence Act. Under section 30 of The Evidence Act confession of a co-accused can only be taken into consideration but it cannot be treated as a substantive evidence and can be pressed into service in support of other evidences. PW 1 Noor Alam made confession and same was recorded by PW 6 Md Sabir Ahmed, Magistrate, First Class. PW 6 stood on witness box in proof as to the true and voluntary character of confessional statement. Noor Alam, thereafter, became an approver and gave evidence as PW 1 making disclosure of circumstances and event of incident. The evidence of prosecution witnesses lent support and assurance to confessional statement and evidence of approver PW 1. 

 71. Chapter XVI of Penal Code deals with homicidal deaths and other evidences affecting human life. Section 299 of Penal Code defines the offence of culpable homicide. This section states when culpable homicide amounts to murder. In Penal Code culpable homicide is used in generic term and is exhaustively sub-divided into two species, namely, culpable homicide amounting to Murder (section 300 clauses 1, 2, 3 and 4) and culpable homicide not amounting to Murder(section 299 and Exceptions to section 300). The offence will amount to murder if the conditions laid down in section 300 is satisfied. If the offence comes under section 299 or under one or other of the Exceptions to section 300 it will be culpable homicide not amounting to Murder. Culpable homicide is murder when the party inflicting the injury does it with the intention that it would cause death or with the knowledge that it may do so. It will not be murder if the case falls within any of the Exceptions. Where there is neither intention nor knowledge nor likelihood that the injury will or can result in death, the offence would be neither murder nor culpable homicide not amounting to murder but it would be voluntarily causing grievous hurt or hurt and conviction in such case would be either under section 325 or 326 according to the nature of the weapons used or under section 323 of the Penal Code. In considering whether the offence is murder or culpable homicide not amounting to murder the manner of causing injuries as testified by prosecution witnesses, nature of the injury caused on part of the body when they were caused, weapons used in commission of offence and conduct of the accused are relevant factors. 

 72. Section 34 of Penal Code lays down principles of Joint liability in doing of a criminal act. The essence of that liability is to be found in the existence of common intention animating the accused leading to the doing of a criminal act in furtherance of such intention. The distinct feature of section 34 is the element of "participation in action". The common intention implies acting in concert, existence of a pre-arranged plan and pre-supposes a pre concert. There must be prior meeting of minds. The prior concert or meeting of minds may be determined by the conduct of the offenders unfolding itself during course of action and the declaration made by them just before mounting the attack. It can, also, develop at the spur of the moment. There must be pre-arrangement or premeditated concert. Criminal sharing overt or covert act by active presence or by distant direction making out a certain measure of jointness in the commission of act is the essence of section 34 of The Penal Code. Leading case on section 34 of Penal Code is Barendra Kumar Ghosh vs Emperor, AIR 1925 PC 1. The authority speaks of "Participation in action". Supreme Court of Pakistan in Hassan vs State, 1969 Criminal Law Journal 1007 held that mere presence of accused is not sufficient for conviction under section 34 of Penal Code and proof of some overt act on part of each accused in furtherance of common intention is necessary. The Judicial Committee of Privy Council in Mahbub Shah vs Emperor, AIR 1945 PC 118 took into account the import of section 34 of Penal Code. Privy Council held that it is clear that common intention within the meaning of section 34 implies a pre-arranged plan. To convict the accused of an offence applying section 34 it should be proved that the criminal act was done in concert pursuant to the pre-arranged plan. It is no doubt difficult, if not impossible, to procure direct evidence to prove the intention of an individual. It has to be inferred from his act or conduct or other relevant circumstances of the case. Import of section 34 of the Penal Code came up for consideration before our Appellate Division in Chand Mia alias Chan Mia Mondal and others vs State, 42 DLR (AD) 3. In this case Barendra Kumar Ghosh vs Emperor, AIR 1925 PC 1 had been, also, considered. In the said case charge under sections 302/34 could not be sustained and the same stood set aside and conviction was altered to section 302 from sections 302/34 of The Penal Code. 

 73. A close analysis of evidences of PWs 1, 3, 4, 5, 7, 9, 10 and 14 clearly indicates that the prosecution could not make out a case that condemned prisoners and appellants and other convicts in furtherance of common intention to kill deceased Khaled assembled in the factory of condemned prisoner Ershad Ali Sikder and shared common intention in commission of murder. Common intention on the part of all accused persons is very much absent. No evidence came forth that there had been prior concert or prior meeting and or pre-plan or there had been subsequent development of common intention amongst accused persons to wipe out Munir (PW 3) and Khaled. Charge of sections 302/34 and 325/34, thus, fell and conviction of offence of sections 302/34 and 325/34 became unsustainable. 

 75. It has earlier been stated that the testimony of eye-witnesses, PWs 1, 3, 4, 5, 7, 9, 10 and 14 fixing condemned prisoner Ershad Ali Sikder as author of death to Khaled is consistent. On scrutiny and assessment of testimonies of above prosecution witnesses and a totality of fact and circumstances of the case we are of this dispassionate view that prosecution could succeed by substantially proving charge of offence of section 302 of Penal Code against condemned prisoner Ershad Ali Sikder beyond all Reasonable doubt. Chain of evidence is so complete that' it does not leave any reasonable doubt for a conclusion consistent with his innocence and, on the other hand, it only points out within all human probability that it is condemned prisoner Ershad Ali Sikder who is the culprit and who caused that death of unfortunate Khaled-Ershad Ali Sikder committed murder of highest degree and section 302 of Penal Code is squarely attracted to his case. 

 76. It has been, also, stated that evidence of PW 1 and other eye-witnesses PWs 3, 4, 5, 7, 10 and 14 connecting Faruque alias Jamai Faruque, LM Liaquat Ali Lashkar, Idris Jamai and Nasir Khan are discrepant and inconsistent in proof of charge of offence of section 302 of Penal Code and we hold that prosecution could not, prove charge of section 302 of Penal Code against them beyond Reasonable doubt and Benefit of Reasonable doubt is to be given to them. Learned trial Judge was not justified in awarding conviction of offence of section 302 of Penal Code upon Faruque alias Jamai Faruque, LM Liaquat Ali Lashkar, Idris Jamai and Nasir Khan Khan and conviction and sentence passed upon them are liable to be set aside. 

 77. This takes us to question whether Ershad Ali Sikder, Faruque alias Jamai Faruque, LM Liaquat Ali Lashkar and Nasir Khan, on legal evidences and materials on record and, also, fact and circumstances of case can be convicted of charge of section 325 of Penal Code. 

 78. It has been noted earlier that evidences of PWs 1, 3, 4, 5, 7, 9, 10 and 14 in connecting Ershad Ali Sikder, Faruque alias Jamai Faruque, LM Liaquat Ali Lashkar and Nasir Khan are consistent in respect of causing injury of grievous nature on injured Monir (PW 3). No ambiguity in their testimonies are manifested and they are found guilty of offence of section 325 of Penal Code and conviction under section 325 of Penal Code can be very much awarded upon them and they are accordingly found guilty of offence of section 325 of Penal Code and convicted there under. 

 81. A meticulous analysis of testimonies of PWs 3, 5, 7, 9, 10 and 14 reveals that prosecution could not bring home charge of section 325 of Penal Code against alleged injured witness Syed Chainul Islam Chayan (PW 4). Even PW 4 did not state in his evidence that he sustained injury following aggression on his person by accused persons. 

 84. True it is that the above convicts were absconders but abscondence by itself does not necessarily lead to a firm conclusion of guilty mind. Even an innocent man may feel panicky and to evade arrest and trial may abscond when suspected of grave crime like murder. The act of abscondence is no doubt a relevant piece of evidence to be considered along with other evidences but its value should always depend under circumstances of each case. Abscondence can scarcely be held as a determining link in completing the chain of circumstantial evidence which must admit of no other reasonable hypothesis than that of guilt of accused. 

 85. It emerged from discussion of evidences of prosecution witness that prosecution failed to bring home charge of sections 325/34 of Penal Code against Md Mannan alias Mona alias Fancy Mona, Ashraf Boro Miah, Ayub Ali Munshi and Kuju Altaf alias Altaf and other persons beyond Reasonable doubt and in view of that we are inclined to give them Benefit of doubt and they are entitled to be graced with a verdict of acquittal. 

 91. Imposition of sentence upon Faruque alias Jamai Faruque, LM Liaquat Ali Lashkar and Nasir Khan shall commensurate with the gravity of offence, nature of criminal intent and manner of perpetration of crime. Taking into stock the criminality and depravity of Faruque alias Jamai Faruque, LM Liaquat Ali Lashkar and Nasir Khan and clinching evidences connecting them in offence we are of this dispassionate view that sentence of Seven (7) years Imprisonment is to be imposed upon them and they shall, also, be liable to pay a fine of Taka 5,000 each and in default of payment of fine they are to suffer Rigorous Imprisonment for one (1) year more.
